questions.q: The editorial quotes the dictum: “Since wars begin in the minds of men, it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be constructed.” What does it conclude?
options: More weapons are needed for defence
Not quite. The article says: Violence done in religion’s name must be answered by correcting the misreadings of scripture behind it.
Borders should be closed
Not quite. The article says: Violence done in religion’s name must be answered by correcting the misreadings of scripture behind it.
Religion should be kept out of schools
Not quite. The article says: Violence done in religion’s name must be answered by correcting the misreadings of scripture behind it.
Violence done in religion’s name must be answered by correcting the misreadings of scripture behind it
Yes. Minds are to be re-engineered along peaceful lines.
questions.rationale: “The terrorist phenomenon is based on misinterpretation of the scriptures. It can be eradicated only by universally publicising the right interpretation of the Islamic texts.”

questions.article: On the Other Side of Death
questions.q: The article gathers the last words of Alexander, Napoleon and Harun al-Rasheed. What do they have in common?
options: Each was proud of his conquests to the end
Not quite. The article says: Men of the greatest worldly success ended feeling they had failed and found no peace.
Each blamed his generals
Not quite. The article says: Men of the greatest worldly success ended feeling they had failed and found no peace.
Men of the greatest worldly success ended feeling they had failed and found no peace
Right. The time to come to one’s senses is before death.
Each asked for a grand tomb
Not quite. The article says: Men of the greatest worldly success ended feeling they had failed and found no peace.
questions.rationale: “Most of the ‘successful’ men of this world have breathed their last overwhelmed with the feeling that they have been the greatest of failures.”

questions.q: “It is only human to err.” What, according to the article, is the glory of man?
options: That he never admits a mistake
Not quite. The article says: That he repents after a mistake and turns back – a “U-turn” that raises him.
That he forgets his errors quickly
Not quite. The article says: That he repents after a mistake and turns back – a “U-turn” that raises him.
That he repents after a mistake and turns back – a “U-turn” that raises him
Yes. God promises to accept repentance.
That he is stronger than the angels
Not quite. The article says: That he repents after a mistake and turns back – a “U-turn” that raises him.
questions.rationale: “The glory of man is that he repents after he makes a mistake… It is an intellectual process that leads man to higher levels of personality development.”

questions.q: The universe shows no flaw. What does the article infer about what God has in store for man?
options: A perfect Creator will not leave His gifts incomplete – desires given here will find fulfilment in Paradise
Well reasoned. Hence one should never despair of His mercy.
Only the flawless will be rewarded
Not quite. The article says: A perfect Creator will not leave His gifts incomplete – desires given here will find fulfilment in Paradise.
Man must perfect the world himself
Not quite. The article says: A perfect Creator will not leave His gifts incomplete – desires given here will find fulfilment in Paradise.
Nothing more can be expected than this life
Not quite. The article says: A perfect Creator will not leave His gifts incomplete – desires given here will find fulfilment in Paradise.
questions.rationale: “When God is perfect, God’s bounties cannot be imperfect… these bounties will reach their perfection only in Paradise.”

questions.q: Some say the things of nature are parts of God Himself. What does the article give as the Quran’s teaching?
options: They have always existed without cause
Not quite. The article says: They are not parts of God; they are created at His command.
They are illusions
Not quite. The article says: They are not parts of God; they are created at His command.
They are not parts of God; they are created at His command
Correct. Sun, moon and stars are creations.
They are lesser gods
Not quite. The article says: They are not parts of God; they are created at His command.
questions.rationale: “According to the Quran, these things are not part of God, but are created at His command.”

questions.q: Descartes said, “I think, therefore I exist.” How does the article extend this reasoning?
options: Only philosophers can know God
Not quite. The article says: The “I” is known by perception, not sight; in the same way God can be known though unseen.
Whatever we think of must exist
Not quite. The article says: The “I” is known by perception, not sight; in the same way God can be known though unseen.
The “I” is known by perception, not sight; in the same way God can be known though unseen
Yes. To deny Him would be like denying one’s own self.
Thinking is more real than the body
Not quite. The article says: The “I” is known by perception, not sight; in the same way God can be known though unseen.
questions.rationale: “We shall have to believe in God on the basis of the same logical principle which Descartes employed to know himself.”

questions.article: God Has Created You for a Higher Purpose
questions.q: When a plan of yours is prevented from working out, how does the article suggest you read it?
options: As bad luck to be waited out
Not quite. The article says: As a hint that God intends something higher for you, and a call to rethink.
As a punishment for past wrongs
Not quite. The article says: As a hint that God intends something higher for you, and a call to rethink.
As proof that you lack ability
Not quite. The article says: As a hint that God intends something higher for you, and a call to rethink.
As a hint that God intends something higher for you, and a call to rethink
Right. Moses was not meant to stay in Pharaoh’s palace.
questions.rationale: “If your plans do not get fulfilled, it is an indication from God. It tells you that He has created you for something bigger than what you are presently involved in.”

questions.q: The article separates a mission’s permanent ideology from its practical strategy. How does it apply this to the early history of Islam?
options: The battles are the principle; belief is the strategy
Not quite. The article says: The oneness of God is the lasting principle; the battles were responses to the conditions of the time.
Both are permanent and unchanging
Not quite. The article says: The oneness of God is the lasting principle; the battles were responses to the conditions of the time.
Neither has any relevance today
Not quite. The article says: The oneness of God is the lasting principle; the battles were responses to the conditions of the time.
The oneness of God is the lasting principle; the battles were responses to the conditions of the time
Yes. As civil disobedience was to Gandhi’s non-violence.
questions.rationale: “The verses of the Quran that talk of tawheed are part of the eternal ideology of Islam, while the verses that talk of qital… related to the practical strategy adopted in response to prevailing conditions.”

questions.q: In a storm at sea a little girl went on playing with her dolls. Why was she not afraid?
options: She did not know there was a storm
Not quite. The article says: Her father was the captain, and she trusted he would not let the ship sink.
Her father was the captain, and she trusted he would not let the ship sink
Exactly. Such is a believer’s trust in God.
She had been told to stay calm
Not quite. The article says: Her father was the captain, and she trusted he would not let the ship sink.
She had sailed many times before
Not quite. The article says: Her father was the captain, and she trusted he would not let the ship sink.
questions.rationale: “‘You know, my father is the Captain of this ship. He is not going to let it sink.’… The same is true of a person of faith.”

questions.q: A scholar said he understood the chapter “The Passage of Time” from an ice-seller’s cry in the market. What was the lesson?
options: Life, like ice, is melting away; the time left must be used well
Well read. Faith, good deeds and counsel to truth and patience.
Merchants deserve sympathy
Not quite. The article says: Life, like ice, is melting away; the time left must be used well.
Ice should be sold quickly
Not quite. The article says: Life, like ice, is melting away; the time left must be used well.
Summer is a time of trial
Not quite. The article says: Life, like ice, is melting away; the time left must be used well.
questions.rationale: “‘O, people! Have mercy on one whose assets are melting away!’… just as the ice melts and reduces, similarly the lifespan given to man is fast passing away.”
